workflow_configuration.task_objective: Diagnose and resolve undocumented, non-deterministic defects — Heisenbugs, race conditions, memory leaks, distributed-state divergence — through disciplined falsification rather than intuition. The systematic approach: treat every bug as a scientific problem in which the failing system is the experiment, observations are evidence, and beliefs are hypotheses to be disproven. Operating invariants: (1) never change code before the failure is characterized — a fix applied to an undiagnosed bug is a hypothesis deployed to production; (2) preserve the crime scene — capture state (core dumps, heap snapshots, logs, traces, metrics) before any restart, redeploy, or cleanup destroys it; (3) one variable at a time — every experiment changes exactly one thing and predicts its outcome in writing before running; (4) the root cause is established only when you can turn the bug ON and OFF — reproduce it via the causal mechanism and make it vanish via the fix, with an explanation that accounts for every observed symptom, including why it was intermittent; (5) a resolved bug ends with a regression test that fails on the old code, plus the detection (alert, assertion, invariant check) that would have caught it in minutes instead of weeks. Completion standard: the explanation is mechanistic (WHY, at the level of memory model, scheduler, network, or protocol — not "it stopped happening"), the fix addresses the mechanism rather than suppressing the symptom, and residual risk (same pattern elsewhere in the codebase) has been searched for and dispositioned.

diagnostic_triage.phase_1_symptom_isolation: 1. Freeze evidence before touching anything: snapshot logs, metrics, traces, core dumps, heap profiles, thread dumps, and the exact build/config/environment identifiers (commit SHA, container image digest, feature flags, instance IDs, clock skew) of the failing state. In distributed systems, capture from ALL involved nodes with timestamps, and record the timebase — you cannot correlate what you did not collect. 2. Write the symptom statement precisely and quantitatively: what is observed vs. what is expected, first-seen time, frequency (1-in-N requests, N times/day), affected population (which tenants, shards, regions, versions), and correlation with load, deploys, time-of-day, or data shape. "Sometimes slow" is not a symptom; "p99 latency rises from 80ms to 9s on shard-7 during compaction, starting with build 4812" is. 3. Establish the delta: what changed at first occurrence — code, dependencies, config, traffic, data volume, infrastructure, certificates, quotas. Diff against the last known-good state (bisect builds/configs if the boundary is unclear). Absence of a known change is itself evidence (points toward load/data-dependent thresholds). 4. Observe without perturbing — Heisenbug discipline: prefer observation channels that do not alter timing or memory layout: already-emitted telemetry, sampling profilers, hardware watchpoints, kernel/OS tracing (eBPF, DTrace, ETW), flight-recorder modes, and post-mortem artifacts, over stepping debuggers and added print statements, which change scheduling and layout and can mask races. If instrumentation must be added, make it non-blocking and constant-cost (lock-free ring buffer, sampled), add it everywhere symmetric (not just the suspected path), and record that the observation channel changed — if the bug's frequency shifts when observation changes, that shift is itself a clue pointing to timing or layout sensitivity. 5. Reproduce the environment, not just the code: same build artifacts, same flags, same data shape, same concurrency level, comparable latency between components. For non-deterministic bugs, script a reproduction harness that runs the scenario in a tight loop and records per-run outcomes — a 1-in-500 reproduction under harness beats a 1-in-day reproduction in production. Measure and record the base reproduction rate; it is the denominator for every later experiment. 6. Shrink the surface while the symptom persists: remove components, disable features, reduce dataset, and drop concurrency step by step, verifying after each removal (against the base rate, with enough trials to be statistically meaningful) that the symptom survives. Stop shrinking at the smallest configuration that still fails — that is the input to phase 3. If a removal makes the bug vanish, do not celebrate: record it as a boundary observation and put the component back; vanishing under change is correlation, not diagnosis. 7. Exit criterion: a written failure characterization — precise symptom, environment fingerprint, reproduction procedure with measured rate, evidence archive location, and the change-delta — sufficient for another engineer to reproduce the failure without you.
diagnostic_triage.phase_2_hypothesis_generation: 1. Generate breadth before depth: enumerate candidate causes across every layer before investigating any single one — application logic, library/framework versions, runtime (GC, JIT, allocator), OS/kernel (scheduler, file descriptors, memory pressure), network (retries, timeouts, partitions, load balancer behavior), data (encoding, size outliers, schema drift), time (clock skew, DST, leap seconds, timer resolution), configuration, and hardware. For each candidate, write one line: the mechanism, and what it predicts that other candidates do not. 2. Demand mechanism, not vibe: every hypothesis must name a concrete causal chain ("connection pool exhausts because retries multiply under timeout, so acquisition blocks, so the event loop stalls") and must explain the observed distribution — why intermittent, why this shard, why after 40 minutes. A hypothesis that does not explain the intermittency pattern is incomplete for a non-deterministic bug. 3. Rank by evidence fit first, then prior probability, then test cost: (a) how many observed facts does it explain, and — weighted heavier — is it CONTRADICTED by any fact already in hand (a single contradiction eliminates); (b) base rates: recent changes, configuration, and misuse of concurrency primitives are more common than compiler bugs, kernel bugs, or cosmic rays — extraordinary hypotheses ("the database is broken") require ordinary ones to be eliminated first; (c) cheap discriminating tests move a hypothesis up the queue even if it is less likely, because elimination is progress. 4. Seek discriminators, not confirmations: for the top hypotheses, design the observation that would DISTINGUISH them — an experiment whose predicted outcome differs between hypothesis A and B. State each prediction in writing before looking ("if it is pool exhaustion, acquisition wait time spikes before latency does; if it is GC, safepoint pauses align with the spikes"). Evidence consistent with everything is worth nothing. 5. Keep a hypothesis ledger: every candidate with status (open / eliminated-by-X / confirmed-pending-falsification), the evidence for and against, and the experiments run with their predicted vs. actual outcomes. The ledger prevents re-investigating eliminated causes, exposes when you are stuck in one layer, and is the handoff artifact if the investigation transfers. Re-read it whenever stuck: contradictions between entries usually point at the wrong assumption. 6. Audit assumptions explicitly when the ledger empties: list what you believe without having verified — "the config that is deployed is the config in git", "the two services see the same clock", "this code path is the only writer", "the library is the version in the lockfile" — and verify each directly. Non-deterministic bugs live disproportionately in false assumptions, because the assumed-true is never instrumented. 7. Exit criterion: a ranked shortlist (typically two or three) of mechanistic hypotheses, each with a written discriminating prediction and a designed falsification experiment, plus a ledger of everything already eliminated and by what evidence.
diagnostic_triage.phase_3_falsification: 1. Aim to disprove, not to confirm: for each shortlisted hypothesis, build the cheapest artifact that can produce a clean CONTRADICTION. The MRE's purpose is epistemic — it is the instrument that lets a hypothesis fail decisively. Design the experiment so that at least one possible outcome would falsify the hypothesis; if no outcome could, the experiment is theater. 2. Build the MRE by extraction or reconstruction, whichever is cheaper: (a) extraction — start from the phase-1 minimal failing configuration and keep deleting (code, dependencies, data, processes) while the failure persists; or (b) reconstruction — write the suspected mechanism from scratch in a scratch project (two tasks, one lock, one shared map; or two services, one retry policy) and check whether the failure emerges. Reconstruction is the stronger evidence: if the isolated mechanism reproduces the signature, the mechanism is sufficient; if it refuses to fail, the hypothesis is missing an ingredient — itself a finding. 3. Make the non-determinism tractable inside the MRE — force the interleaving instead of waiting for it: model-check or exhaustively explore schedules where tooling exists (loom for Rust concurrency, TLA+/lite for protocols, deterministic-simulation frameworks for distributed logic); inject targeted delays/yields at suspected race windows to widen them; run under schedulers and stress that amplify (thread-count sweeps, CPU pinning, single-core execution, fault injection, network partition simulation); use record-replay (rr, time-travel debuggers) so one captured failure can be replayed exactly, repeatedly. A race you can force on demand is diagnosed; one you wait for is not. 4. Judge outcomes against the base rate, not anecdotes: define in advance how many clean runs count as "does not reproduce" given the phase-1 rate (if the bug fires 1-in-100, thirty clean runs prove nothing). Record predicted vs. actual for every run batch. An MRE that fails to reproduce eliminates nothing by itself — it bounds where the necessary ingredient lives (in what you removed). 5. Treat vanishing-under-observation as data: if the failure disappears when instrumentation is added or optimization levels change, the hypothesis space collapses toward timing sensitivity, memory layout (uninitialized reads, buffer overruns shifting with layout), or undefined behavior — pivot to sanitizers (ASan/TSan/MSan/UBSan, miri), hardware watchpoints, and record-replay, which observe without the same perturbation. 6. Confirm by bidirectional control before writing the fix: using the MRE, demonstrate the bug turns ON when the mechanism is present and OFF when the single causal ingredient is removed or corrected — with everything else held constant. Then verify the fix in the original system at phase-1 scale and confirm every original symptom (including the intermittency pattern) is accounted for; a fix that "seems to work" without explaining the original distribution is a symptom patch. 7. Bank the artifact: the MRE becomes the regression test (deterministic via the forced interleaving where possible, stress-loop with a statistical bound where not); the causal mechanism gets an invariant check or alert in production; the pattern is searched for across the codebase and each other occurrence is fixed or ticketed. Exit criterion: bug demonstrably ON/OFF under control, fix verified at scale, regression test merged, detection in place, residual occurrences dispositioned, ledger closed with the mechanistic explanation.

domain_specific_heuristics.concurrency: 1. Capture the stuck state first: on suspected deadlock or exhaustion, take thread/task dumps (multiple, seconds apart — a deadlock is frozen across dumps; slow progress is not), the async runtime's task list with await points, lock-graph or monitor information, and pool statistics (in-use, idle, waiters, acquisition wait time) for every pool: threads, connections, semaphores, file descriptors. 2. Distinguish the failure class from the dumps before hypothesizing: true deadlock (circular wait between lock holders — visible as a cycle), async deadlock (a task awaiting a resource that only its own executor thread could release), thread/pool exhaustion (all workers occupied, queue growing, no cycle), livelock (state changing but no progress; dumps differ, throughput zero), and starvation (some waiters never scheduled while others proceed). Each class has a different fix family; misclassifying wastes the investigation. 3. For async deadlocks, hunt the two canonical mechanisms in order: (a) blocking a cooperative executor — synchronous lock, blocking I/O, or a block_on/.Result/.get() inside an async task, which occupies the worker thread so the completion it waits for can never be polled; sweep the codebase for blocking calls reachable from async context (lint rules and runtime detectors exist for most runtimes: BlockHound, tokio-console, asyncio debug mode's slow-callback log); (b) resource cycles across await points — task A holds an async mutex/semaphore permit across an await and waits on B, which needs A's permit; audit every guard held across an await, and every bounded channel where producer and consumer can be the same task pool. 4. For thread/pool exhaustion, follow the arithmetic: measure demand (arrival rate × hold time) against capacity (pool size); find what inflated hold time (a slow downstream, a missing timeout, a retry storm multiplying in-flight work — retries WITHOUT jittered backoff and budgets are the most common amplifier) or what leaked permits (acquisition paths that fail to release on error/cancellation; audit every acquire for a release on all exits, including panic/exception and cancellation). Sweep for sync-over-async bridges: N tasks blocking threads while waiting for work that needs those same threads is exhaustion that presents as deadlock at full load. 5. Reproduce by shrinking the arena: drop pool sizes and worker counts to 1–2 and queue bounds to near zero in a test harness — undersized pools convert 1-in-a-million interleavings into every-run failures. Force suspected interleavings with injected yields/delays at the identified await points; on Rust, model-check the lock/permit protocol with loom; elsewhere use stress harnesses with schedule randomization. 6. Fix by ordering and structure, not by sleeps: establish a global lock/resource acquisition order (and assert it in debug builds); never hold a lock or permit across an await unless proven necessary and cycle-free; give every external wait a timeout and every retry a budget with jittered backoff; make executors' blocking work explicit (spawn_blocking / dedicated pools); size pools from measured demand, and alarm on acquisition wait time — the leading indicator that precedes the outage. A sleep that "fixes" the test is a falsified fix: it narrows the race window and ships the bug.
domain_specific_heuristics.state_corruption: 1. Characterize the corruption before hunting the writer: which fields diverge from expectation, in which direction, how far from the last-known-good, and whether corruption is structural (invariant broken: negative quantity, dangling reference, sum mismatch) or semantic (valid-looking but wrong). Write the violated invariant down as an executable predicate — it becomes both the detector and the regression oracle. 2. Enumerate the writers: in a unidirectional-data-flow architecture there is supposed to be exactly one mutation path (action → dispatcher → store). List every code location that can reach the corrupted state — legitimate reducers, but also the violation channels: direct field assignment bypassing dispatch, shared references handed out by the store and mutated in place (aliasing), stale copies written back (read-modify-write races), out-of-band mutation from callbacks/subscriptions re-entering the store, serialization round-trips, and migrations. In distributed variants: multiple writers to the same key, non-idempotent retried writes, and replays applying stale events. 3. Instrument the choke point, then catch the bypass: add invariant checks and mutation logging (who, what, when, prior value, stack/task context) at the single legitimate write path. If corruption appears WITHOUT a corresponding log entry, a bypass exists — escalate to mechanisms that catch the writer in the act: language-level immutability (freeze/immutable types so illegal writes throw at the write site), hardware watchpoints on the corrupted address, sanitizers for out-of-bounds/UAF writes from unrelated code (memory-unsafe layers), and object-level write barriers or copy-on-write wrappers in managed runtimes. 4. Exploit time-travel where the architecture provides it: with a serial single-writer store, record the action log and replay it — if replay reproduces the corruption, the defect is IN a reducer (deterministic; bisect the action sequence to the offending action, then falsify per phase 3). If replay produces correct state, the corruption entered outside the dispatch path (aliasing, direct write, or concurrency) — the divergence point between replayed and observed state history localizes when. 5. Check the epochs and the edges: for async state machines, verify stale-response protection — late-arriving results must carry the request epoch and be discarded on mismatch (rapid navigation/retry overwriting fresh state with stale is the classic UDF race); verify subscribers receive snapshots or immutable views rather than live references; verify every observed "torn" state (half of update A, half of update B) against non-atomic multi-field commits. 6. Fix at the boundary, then make the violation impossible: correct the offending writer, then close the class — make state types deeply immutable, make the store the sole owner (no leaked mutable references; enforce with the type system where available: Rust ownership, readonly/frozen types), assert the invariant at every commit in debug builds and behind sampling in production, and merge the replay test. A state-corruption fix without a structural guarantee is an invitation for the next bypass.

critical_pitfalls.pitfall: Restarting the service, adding a retry, bumping the pool size, or catching-and-ignoring the exception makes the alarm stop while the mechanism keeps running. Discipline: a fix is legitimate only when it targets the mechanism established by bidirectional control (bug ON/OFF); mitigations are allowed for availability but must be labeled as mitigations with the investigation kept open.

Deciding what the bug is in the first five minutes, then collecting only evidence that agrees. Discipline: write predictions before observations; actively design experiments to disprove the favored hypothesis; keep the ledger honest by recording contradicting evidence with the same weight as supporting evidence; when two facts conflict, the favored hypothesis does not get the tie-break.

Ad-hoc prints perturb timing and layout (masking races), produce unstructured output that cannot be correlated across threads or nodes, get deleted after the incident, and require redeploys that destroy state. Discipline: prefer existing structured telemetry, sampling profilers, kernel tracing, and record-replay; when instrumentation must be added, make it structured, correlated (trace/task IDs), cheap, and permanent — the investigation's instrumentation is the next incident's head start. Corollary: a codebase that can only be debugged by adding prints has an observability defect worth its own ticket.

Applying three plausible fixes at once, or fixing while also upgrading the library. Whatever happens next, you learn nothing — and the shipped combination may contain a new bug. Discipline: one change per experiment, predicted outcome written first, revert before the next candidate.

The bug "hasn't happened since Tuesday" after a low-frequency failure proves nothing (silence is expected under the base rate). Discipline: compute how much failure-free exposure would be statistically meaningful given the measured rate; prefer the forced-reproduction MRE as the arbiter; never close a non-deterministic bug on quiet alone.

"It started when we deployed X" and "it stops when we disable Y" identify suspects, not causes — coincident load shifts, cache warm-up, and layout changes produce the same signatures. Discipline: a suspect graduates only through the phase-3 mechanism test (ON/OFF under control with everything else constant).

Assuming the deployed config matches the repo, the clocks agree, the library matches the lockfile, the cache was invalidated, or "this code can't run twice concurrently" — then never checking. Discipline: when hypotheses run out, the bug is usually inside an assumption; enumerate and verify them directly. Its inverse is equally fatal: blaming the compiler/kernel/database first — extraordinary claims require the ordinary candidates eliminated and an MRE demonstrating the platform defect.

Treating "it doesn't reproduce under the debugger" as bad luck instead of as evidence. Discipline: vanishing-under-observation is a strong signal of timing, layout, or UB sensitivity — reroute immediately to sanitizers, watchpoints, record-replay, and schedule-forcing tools instead of repeating the perturbing observation harder.

Finding A real defect and assuming it is THE defect. Plausible-but-innocent bugs are common in old code paths. Discipline: the accepted cause must explain every symptom — the frequency, the distribution across shards, the onset time; unexplained residue means either a second bug or the wrong diagnosis.

Merging the fix and closing the ticket with no test that fails on the old code, no invariant check, no alert. The same class of bug returns and the next engineer starts from zero. Discipline: no non-deterministic bug is closed without its banked MRE-derived test, its production detection, and a codebase sweep for siblings of the same pattern.

Spending days in application code when the mechanism lives in the allocator, the kernel scheduler, the load balancer's connection reuse, or a data outlier. Discipline: the phase-2 breadth-first enumeration is mandatory before depth; when stuck, re-run it — the layer you have not instrumented is where the bug is hiding.
